edges.what: The four-bar drum break from the middle of 'Amen, Brother' is chopped and rearranged as the main rhythm.
The Amen drum break runs under the verses as the core beat.
The Amen break is sped up and cut into rapid jungle rolls that drive the whole track.
A slowed Amen break loop sits under the song's opening and main groove.
Chopped pieces of the Amen break power the frantic drum section of the song.
Clyde Stubblefield's drum break is one of the layered loops in the beat.
The Funky Drummer break supplies the driving drum loop.
The Funky Drummer break loops under the song as its drum track.
The drum break from the Bobby Byrd record is looped as the song's shuffling beat.
Marley Marl built the beat from the opening drum break of 'Impeach the President'.
The 'Impeach the President' drum break sits under the piano melody.
The Incredible Bongo Band remade The Shadows' instrumental and added the long bongo and drum break that DJs loved.
The Sugarhill Gang rapped over a replayed version of the Bongo Band groove.
The Apache drum and bongo break is looped as the backbone of the beat.
The Apache break and its horn line are sampled throughout the track.
Led Zeppelin rewrote the 1929 country blues about the Mississippi flood into a slow, heavy epic.
John Bonham's opening drum pattern is looped as the main beat.
Bonham's Levee drum intro supplies the beat.
The Levee drums are slowed and looped under the cover of the Paragons song.
The thundering Levee drum sound is sampled as the track's beat.
A studio band replayed Bernard Edwards' 'Good Times' bassline and groove for the whole song.
Flash cuts the 'Good Times' bass groove live on turntables as one of the mix's main beds.
Flash scratches in the Queen bassline and chorus.
Debbie Harry's rap section from 'Rapture' is mixed in, a nod to Blondie name-checking Flash.
The eerie main melody of 'Trans-Europe Express' is replayed on synthesizer.
The rhythm pattern from 'Numbers' is rebuilt on a Roland TR-808 drum machine.
The synth melody from 'Computer Love' is replayed on guitar as the song's main riff, with Kraftwerk's permission.
The robotic rhythm and voice from 'Numbers' are sampled in the beat.
The electro synth riff from 'Clear' is the track's main hook.
A horn stab and chord phrase from the Eddie Johns record are filtered and looped as the song's base.
A short keyboard and vocal phrase from George Duke's song is looped under the track.
The rising keyboard riff from 'Cola Bottle Baby' is chopped into the main hook.
The vocoder chant and synth riff of 'Harder, Better, Faster, Stronger' drive the chorus.
The guitar and drum riff from Breakwater's song is looped as the song's entire riff.
A short loop from the Sister Sledge track underpins the groove before the guitar solo.
Chaka Khan's chorus is sped up into a chipmunk soul loop.
Jamie Foxx sings the hook in Ray Charles' style, reworking the opening lines of 'I Got a Woman'.
The horn fanfare and drums from 'Move On Up' are slowed and looped as the beat.
The sweet 'bound' vocal hook from the Ponderosa Twins record is cut in and out across the song.
Nina Simone recorded a slower, starker version of the anti-lynching song Billie Holiday made famous.
Nina Simone's voice from 'Strange Fruit' is pitched and looped through the song.
The shouted '21st century schizoid man' line and its riff are cut in at the song's peaks.
The 'did you feel like Jesus' backing vocal line is sped up and looped as the hook.
The bouncing synth melody from 'P.Y.T.' is replayed under the beat.
Justin Vernon's stacked, auto-tuned vocal from 'Woods' opens the song and returns as its spine.
Long passages of Gil Scott-Heron's spoken poem are played over the closing track.
Sister Nancy's 'Bam Bam' vocal is used in the song's final section.
Lauryn Hill borrows the 'bam bam' melody and phrasing in the chorus.
A piano and handclap section from 'Sinnerman' is looped as the beat.
Otis Redding turned the 1932 ballad into a slow-building soul song that explodes at the end.
Otis Redding's vocal grunts and lines are chopped into the beat.
The piano and bass run from 'I Want You Back' is looped as the beat.
The heavy bass and drum groove from 'Five to One' is the backbone of the beat, along with Jim Morrison's voice.
The chorus borrows Bowie's descending 'Fame' vocal hook.
Bobby Bland's vocal hook is sped up and looped.
The orphans' chorus from the musical is looped as the hook.
The guitar riff and groove from 'That Lady' carry the whole song.
The dreamy vocal and guitar from 'Silver Soul' are looped as the beat.
Timmy Thomas's organ and drum machine pattern is looped under the song.
Gladys Knight's spoken intro and melody are looped as the beat.
A piece of the Wu-Tang track is sampled, credited on the song.
Lauryn Hill's 'Ex-Factor' vocal is chopped and looped through the beat.
The chorus melody and lyrics borrow from 'Ex-Factor'.
The Charmels' piano line and vocal phrase are looped as the beat.
The Mtume groove and 'juicy' melody are looped as the beat.
The slow trumpet groove from 'Rise' is the backbone of the beat.
The synth and vocal melody from 'Between the Sheets' is looped under the song.
The 'I'm Coming Out' horn and guitar riff powers the beat and chorus.
Snoop redid Slick Rick's story rap line by line in his own voice.
The beat and vocal hook from 'Children's Story' run under the chorus.
The piano and horn riff from Joe Cocker's song is the main riff.
The chorus reworks the hook from The Spinners' 'Sadie'.
Bruce Hornsby's piano riff loops through the whole song.
The 'O-o-h child, things are gonna get easier' line is sung in the chorus.
The bassline from 'Don't Look Any Further' drives the beat.
The same bassline is looped under the song.
The slow keyboard groove from Leon Haywood's song is the base of the beat.
The 'swing down, sweet chariot' chant from 'Mothership Connection' is the hook.
The soft guitar and keyboard groove from 'Footsteps in the Dark' is looped as the beat.
Bob Dorough's Schoolhouse Rock song gives the track its title phrase and hook.
The 'Peg' chorus riff is looped under the verses.
Otis Redding's whistle from the end of 'Dock of the Bay' is cut into the hook.
The synth and vocal groove from '(Not Just) Knee Deep' is the backbone of the track.
The Hall and Oates drum machine and keyboard groove is looped as the beat.
The bassline from 'Walk on the Wild Side' is looped through the song.
The electric piano and bass from 'Mystic Brew' form the smooth loop.
Guitar and vocal pieces from the 10cc song are chopped into the beat.
The Escorts' vocal is chopped so the singers seem to say 'don't cry'.
A soft Jackson 5 vocal phrase is looped and chopped through the track.
The gentle horn and keyboard intro is looped as the beat.
A short guitar figure from the Getz and Bonfá recording is looped by Jay Dee into the beat.
Bobby Caldwell's keyboard and vocal groove is looped as the warm bed of the song.
The vocal line 'since I left you' and string swells are lifted from The Main Attraction's 'Everyday'.
The flute melody from 'Prison Song' is the hook of the beat.
The melody and opening lines of Ginuwine's 'Differences' are reworked in the chorus.
The banjo loop from the Nine Inch Nails instrumental is the base of the beat.
The guitar figure from Luiz Bonfá's 'Seville' is looped under the verses.
The xylophone melody and chorus melody from the Gotye song carry the track.
Dionne Warwick's 'walk on by' vocal line is looped as the hook.
Isaac Hayes stretched the Bacharach and David song into a twelve-minute orchestral soul epic.
The guitar melody from 'Shape of My Heart' loops under the song.
Harry Belafonte's 'day-o' and 'daylight come' calls open and recur in the beat.
Willie Hutch's 'I choose you' vocal and arrangement are looped as the beat.
Dido's first verse and chorus are used as the song's hook.
The guitar riff and Steven Tyler's chorus from 'Dream On' run through the song.
The opening 'two trailer park girls go round the outside' line reworks Malcolm McLaren's chant.
The bass and drum groove from the Labi Siffre song is the beat.
A slowed piece of 'Kiss of Life' gives the beat its hazy loop.
Madlib built the beat from the accordion loop in Daedelus's 'Experience'.
The dark piano phrase from 'Mind Rain' is looped as the beat.
A piano phrase from Ahmad Jamal's 'I Love Music' is looped as the beat.
The chorus and title phrase rework Kurtis Blow's song.
Enya's wordless vocal from 'Boadicea' loops under the whole song.
The chorus melody and lines reuse The Delfonics' song.
Roberta Flack's version turned Lori Lieberman's folk song into a hit.
Lauryn Hill sings the song over a hip-hop drum loop.
Herbie Hancock's piano riff and Freddie Hubbard's trumpet are looped under a new beat.
The bell intro of 'Take Me to the Mardi Gras' is cut and scratched as the beat.
The moody electric piano and drum parts from 'Nautilus' are chopped into the beat.
The Roy Ayers groove and melody are looped as the song's base.
The Audio Two drum break is used as the song's beat.
The slow synth melody and groove from 'Summer Madness' set the beat.
The slow, sad string and horn loop from 'Ike's Rap II' is the bed of the song.
A brooding phrase from Lalo Schifrin's spy score is looped as the beat.
The bassline and drums from Billy Cobham's 'Stratus' drive the track.
A vocal and organ phrase from Jeremy Storch's song is looped in the track.
Vera Hall's 1937 field recording vocal is the song's lead vocal.
Camille Yarbrough's 'we've come a long, long way together' vocal is the hook.
Schoolly D's 'back with another one of those block rockin' beats' line gives the song its title and hook.
The title vocal line is lifted from the Ultramagnetic MCs track.
A guitar squeal from the Breeders song is sampled in the track.
Ray J's vocal is pitched and chopped into ghostly fragments.
The bassline and groove from Sly's song are looped as the beat.
The groove and vocal hook of 'Loose Booty' are the base of the track.
The 'bow wow wow yippie yo yippie yay' chant and groove come from 'Atomic Dog'.
The 'woo! yeah!' shouts and drum break from 'Think (About It)' power the beat.
Bill Withers' 'grandma's hands' vocal and guitar figure open and drive the beat.
The synth and vocal hook from 'Human Nature' is looped in the beat.
The 'Human Nature' groove and melody carry the remix.
Aretha Franklin turned Otis Redding's plea into a demand, adding the spelled-out 'R-E-S-P-E-C-T' and 'sock it to me' backing vocals.
Aretha's vocal and piano phrase are looped as the beat.
Donna Summer's vocal and the pulsing synth sequence from 'I Feel Love' carry the track.
The beat and synth line from 'The Message' run under the remix.
The chorus reworks the 'don't push me 'cause I'm close to the edge' hook.
Run-DMC rapped Aerosmith's song over its drum intro with Steven Tyler and Joe Perry playing on it.
The title phrase and part of the groove come from the Isley Brothers song.
The Mary Jane Girls' 'all night long' vocal hook is looped in the chorus.
The guitar riff from 'My Sharona' is the hook.
Cream turned the solo acoustic blues into a loud, fast electric jam.
Much of Robert Plant's lyric reworks Willie Dixon's song, and Dixon was later credited.
The opening riff and lyrics borrow from 'Killing Floor', and Howlin' Wolf was later credited.
Elmore James electrified the song with the slide guitar triplet riff that became his signature.
Jack White plays Son House's song as a raw slide guitar and drums stomp.
Kurt Cobain closed MTV Unplugged with the old folk song, credited through Lead Belly.
Lonnie Donegan's sped-up skiffle version became a UK hit.
Led Zeppelin rebuilt the gospel blues around a stop-start guitar and vocal riff.
Hendrix turned Dylan's sparse folk song into a layered electric piece.
The Byrds cut Dylan's song down to one verse and added twelve-string guitar and harmonies.
Guns N' Roses turned Dylan's short ballad into an arena rock anthem.
John Cale recorded a piano version using a different set of Cohen's verses.
Jeff Buckley based his electric guitar version on John Cale's arrangement.
Whitney Houston opened with the a cappella first verse and built it into a power ballad.
Beyoncé kept the melody but rewrote the lyrics as a warning instead of a plea.
Beyoncé recorded the song with four young Black country singers, keeping McCartney's guitar part.
Johnny Cash sang Trent Reznor's song with acoustic guitar and piano near the end of his life.
Cash recast the synth song as an acoustic blues.
Nirvana played Bowie's song on MTV Unplugged.
The Beatles recorded the Isley Brothers' version in one take at the end of a long session.
The opening line 'here come old flat-top' and its melody come from Chuck Berry's song.
The melody is Chuck Berry's 'Sweet Little Sixteen' with new surf lyrics, and Berry was later credited.
Led Zeppelin's song is built on Jake Holmes's descending bassline and mood, later credited 'inspired by Jake Holmes'.
The verse melody echoes the New Seekers song, which led to a settlement.
The melody borrows from Neil Innes's song, and Innes was later given a writing credit.
The chord progression and melody of the verse echo 'The Air That I Breathe', and its writers were credited.
A four-chord synth passage from Paul Lansky's computer music piece is looped as the song's core.
The slide guitar and drum loop from Johnny Jenkins' cover of the Dr. John song drives the track.
The riff from the Them song is looped as the main hook.
The Chili Peppers turned Stevie Wonder's clavinet funk into a slap bass rock song.
Rage replayed the electro track with guitar, bass and drums.
Megadeth played the punk song as speed metal, with Steve Jones guesting on guitar.
Johnny Cash took the melody and many lines from Gordon Jenkins' song, later settled with Jenkins.
Elvis's fast rock version changed the lyrics and drew from Freddie Bell and the Bellboys' stage take.
Elvis's first Sun single sped up Crudup's blues into early rockabilly.
Hank Williams built his yodeling version on Emmett Miller's recording of the old song.
Woody Guthrie set his new lyric to the melody of the Carter Family's 'When the World's on Fire'.
Chris Stapleton slowed the George Jones country hit into a blues and soul ballad.
Sturgill Simpson recast the grunge song as a slow, string-backed country ballad.
Missy Elliott's 'Get Ur Freak On' hook appears in one of the track's many beat switches.
The salsa intro and horns from El Gran Combo's song open the track.
The salsa horn line from Jerry Rivera's song is the main hook.
The 'zamina mina eh eh, waka waka eh eh' chant comes from Golden Sounds' song.
Toni Braxton's chorus is looped as the hook.
Santana turned Tito Puente's cha-cha into a rock song with organ and electric guitar.
The Clash played Toots' reggae song as fast punk.
The Clash stretched Junior Murvin's falsetto reggae song into a six-minute punk reggae piece.
Clapton's laid-back version took the song to number one in the US.
The synth riff from the ABBA song is the main hook, used with Benny and Björn's permission.
The Under Pressure bassline is looped through the song, and Queen and Bowie were later credited.
The Stones built their chorus on the Staple Singers' gospel refrain.
Andrew Loog Oldham's orchestra recorded an orchestral take on the Stones song.
The string loop from the orchestral version runs through the whole song, and Jagger and Richards were credited.
The chorus melody echoes 'Misery Business', and Hayley Williams and Josh Farro were later added as writers.
The bridge melody echoes 'Cruel Summer', and Taylor Swift, Jack Antonoff and St. Vincent were credited.
The chorus cadence follows the 'I'm too sexy' vocal rhythm, and Right Said Fred are credited.
The guitar riff from 'Every Breath You Take' loops under the song.
The melody and chord pattern of 'Pastime Paradise' are replayed as the beat and hook.
The riff from 'Super Freak' is looped as the beat.
The pre-chorus melody echoes 'No Scrubs', and TLC's writers were added to the credits.
The 'uh-oh' horn fanfare from the Chi-Lites song is the hook.
The organ bass and house groove of 'Show Me Love' is interpolated under the track.
The chorus reworks the 'they don't love you like I love you' line from 'Maps'.
Soft Cell turned the northern soul song into a synth pop hit.
The two-note synth riff from Soft Cell's version drives the beat.
The 'mama-se mama-sa ma-ma-coo-sa' chant reworks Manu Dibango's hook.
The 'mama-se mama-sa' chant from Jackson's song closes the track.
The guitar riff echoes INXS's song, and its writers were added to the credits.
The Gap Band's writers were added to the credits after similarities to 'Oops Upside Your Head' were raised.
The Weeknd recast the Michael Jackson song as a moody, echoing ballad.
The keyboard and vocal hook of the Japanese city pop song is looped as the base.
The piano chords of 'Bennie and the Jets' are replayed as the song's main loop.
Lines and melody from the Beatles song are reworked in the lyrics.
The slow bass and guitar groove and chorus melody follow the Bootsy Collins song, and Collins is credited.
Rihanna sang the Tame Impala song over nearly the original backing track.
The chorus borrows lyrics from the Souls of Mischief song, and they are credited.
Lana Del Rey covered Sublime's song, which itself was built on Gershwin's 'Summertime'.
The chugging guitar riff from 'Edge of Seventeen' is looped as the beat.
The chord progression and groove of 'Ain't No Mountain High Enough' are sampled under the song.
A soul vocal and keyboard loop from The Main Ingredient song carries the beat.
Sinéad O'Connor's version of the Prince-written song became a worldwide hit.
PinkPantheress's vocal and melody from 'Just for Me' form the hook of the drill track.
